candidates.explanation: Best guess, because the snippet elides the body of this method. AuthService.refreshToken correctly passes both the session id and the presented hash as conditions, so a replayed token should match zero rows and return null. Replay succeeding suggests the update's where-clause drops the `hash` condition and filters only on `id`. The old token then always matches and the hash is rewritten. The `result.affected` check and the follow-up `findOne` may also look up the session by id alone.

This is the Mongo equivalent. If the `findOneAndUpdate` filter uses only the id, or doesn't apply the hash condition correctly, a stale refresh token still matches and gets rotated again. The body is elided, so I can't confirm it.

The caller depends entirely on `updateByHash` returning null for a stale hash. It performs no explicit `session.hash === data.hash` check of its own. If the repository filter is loose, nothing else rejects the replayed token. This is less likely to be the root cause, since the visible logic looks correct.

fix.description: Make updateByHash filter on both `id` and `hash`, for example `this.sessionRepository.update({ id: Number(conditions.id), hash: conditions.hash }, payload)`. Return null when `affected` is 0. Apply the same fix to the document repository with `findOneAndUpdate({ _id: conditions.id, hash: conditions.hash }, payload, { new: true })`. Optionally add an explicit `session.hash` comparison in AuthService.refreshToken as defense in depth.
